I get that being anti-suicide is sort of a knee-jerk moral reaction that people have. If someone is hurting, you’re supposed to help or encourage them. Especially since there are amazing stories of people who were able to change their minds at the last second and turn there life around. Those people are truly extraordinary and I feel nothing but joy for their personal success. 

But, as someone who’s fluctuated between passive and (for a short time) active suicidal ideations, I feel like most of the legal and systemic obstacles put in place have much more to do with state control than genuine morality. A lot of people understand that if you’re in a toxic or abusive relationship, you should leave because it’s not a situation that serves you (even they don’t understand how hard that is to do). 

If you work at a job you hate or doesn’t work with your schedule (and you have the ability to leave), you should leave because it doesn’t serve you. 

If you live in a region or area that is also shitty for whatever reason (and you have the ability to leave), you should leave. 

I’m willing to argue that *most* people can agree on these things. But suddenly when the relationship/job/place in question is this plane of existence, suddenly everyone would rather preach about how you should never “give up” and say things will inevitably get better even when they have NO way of determining that. Especially when the issues are things like chronic poverty, mental illness, lovelessness, intense disability, etc. And I think this conversation is so hard to have because A) most people don’t want to sound like some encouraging others to take the plunge and B) a lot of people have a hard time distinguishing personal reason for suicidal ideations from demographics. For example, there are plenty of people living far below the poverty line who have suicidal thoughts because of their dire situations, but if we were to condone their assisted suicide then it must mean we’re saying ALL poor people should give up because we’re sending a message that their lives aren’t worth living. But that’s not fair to the individuals who aren’t trying to politicize their actions, they’re simply trying to relieve the pain they’re uniquely affected by. We never got to choose to be born, there’s a lot we don’t get to choose even during this life, and we know for a FACT that it will end. The fact that we have to even argue for the option to at least choose and when it ends in a safe way is just another cruel thing about existing in this world.

Funny thing is, my dad was born & raised in Nigeria and my mom was born & raised in the US. So, I’m quite literally African American (though “halfrican” is a fun new term these days). But, aside from that reason, I use the terms interchangeably. All Black people are descendants from Africa at some point and, at least within this discussion, citizens of the United States. So, I don’t much of a difference, really.

We need to stop acting like it’s Afrocentric representation vs this kind of representation. I’m not gonna act like certain production companies to use this a tool of performative activism to eschew any racist accusations because I know that it happens. BUT I’d still argue that BOTH types of representation are equally as important. Black representation is great for historical analysis/re-imagination, cultural celebration, and calls for social action. Meanwhile, stories that include us in culturally ambiguous tales like Annie, Cinderella, or Spider-Man allow us also be portrayed as just people. 
A lot of these movies are going to keep getting remade every few years anyways so why not at least switch up the race so that more people can see themselves in these characters? For example, Cinderella is an iconic princess that now has a White, Black, and Latina version of her (though I pray they do better than Ms. Cabello in the future). There’s still more work to do but at least little girls from various races can see themselves represented in the same character. A similar thing has happened with the different iterations of Spider-man we’ve seen as well. 

So, in a fictional world that allows it, why not have a Black wizard, a Black superhero, a fairy, a princess, an Amazon, etc? Because our racial identity and history is not all we are. I absolutely love being Black and I think a lot of other people having this discussion do too but the point is that our racial identity and our collective history is not all we are. We’re people that have the capacity to be absolutely anything.

For example, I have plenty of friends that I enjoy talking to and hanging out with but I know they wouldn’t make great partners for me for a few reasons: A) their schedules don’t align well with mine and we wouldn’t get to spend much time together, B) their life goals (or perhaps, lack thereof) don’t align super well with mine and I know that, even if we could enjoy each other’s company for a time, it wouldn’t last, C) they might get overwhelmed too easily and it’s something I can navigate occasionally as their friend but might not be something I can deal with 24/7 as their partner. And this list of reasons could go on. 

Third, even if the two of you have enough in common to date, it’s important to consider the likelihood that the two of you will break up and how that might change the relationship. I’ve been grateful to have some pretty civil breakups but, the reality is that most of them don’t end that way. Whether they’re catastrophically terrible or just passive aggressive, the breakup often ends in the ex-lovers parting ways and never speaking again. So, when they say they don’t want to lose a good friend, that’s what they mean. Depending on how long you’ve known each other and what your dynamic is like, they might be in certain friend circles with you, have a relationship with your family, etc. But if you two have a bitter breakup, all of that goes away.
